extracted.intended_audience: novelists and authors considering adapting their books into film or television screenplays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors deciding whether to adapt their own novel into a screenplay and how to approach the adaptation process, including pros/cons, industry perspective, and practical next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does writing my own screenplay help land a TV/movie deal?
rubrics_metrics.description: Question of whether adapting your novel yourself will help secure a film or TV deal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer: maybe. No two situations are alike; adapting can be a great creative exercise but does not necessarily move you further toward a deal if you haven't already gotten one. It's not the traditional order (book → screenplay → deal). If you already have a deal, deciding whether to adapt yourself is a different, potentially helpful consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative Control
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapting your own novel gives you the opportunity to have more creative control over how plot and characters are portrayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can ensure faithfulness to original story, themes, and nuances, and make subtle adjustments to align the script with the book’s tone and message to create a more authentic adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep Understanding of the Source Material
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors possess the most knowledge of their own stories — characters, themes, and intricate plot details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This deep knowledge helps showcase important subplots, themes, and character arcs that an outside screenwriter might overlook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal Satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing your work brought to screen can be a deeply satisfying experience for an author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors get to see characters embodied, settings visualized, and stories reach new audiences — providing a different sense of achievement than publishing a book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of Screenwriting Experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Many novelists lack the specific skills required for screenwriting; the two mediums are significantly different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screenwriting emphasizes visual storytelling, concise dialogue, and film-style pacing. Novel techniques like interiority and extended narrative descriptions do not translate directly, and this skill gap can make adaptation challenging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and Effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapting a novel into a screenplay is a time-consuming project that requires substantial revision to meet industry standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For authors juggling new books or other projects, writing and repeatedly revising a screenplay can be overwhelming and may detract from literary output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can be too close to their work, making it difficult to cut or change scenes for the screen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Over-attachment to characters, scenes, or subplots may hinder necessary structural and pacing changes for a successful screenplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed Receptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Author-adapted works receive highly variable responses — some are critically acclaimed while others fail with audiences or box office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include Gillian Flynn’s Gone Girl as a success and various Stephen King adaptations as both hits and flops, illustrating that author involvement is not a guarantee of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration with Screenwriters
rubrics_metrics.description: The industry often prefers professional screenwriters to adapt novels, sometimes collaborating with the original author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combines the author’s story knowledge with a screenwriter’s visual storytelling expertise and can lead to faithful yet screen-effective adaptations. Example: Neil Gaiman collaborating with screenwriters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and Training
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors interested in adapting should gain a solid understanding of screenwriting through classes, workshops, and books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended resources listed include The Black List, Done Deal Professional/Tracking Board, Script Magazine, SimplyScripts, Screenwriting U, and John August.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeking Feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should seek critique from experienced screenwriters and industry professionals to refine their scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshopping in screenplay groups or with mentors provides constructive criticism to help scripts meet industry standards. Suggested groups: Stage 32, Scriptwriters Network, The Script Lab, Women in Film and Television (WIFT), The Writers Room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding the Medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must understand the differences between novels and screenplays to build a successful adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that novels allow interiority and detailed description whereas screenplays require concise, action-driven scenes and visual storytelling; craft dialogue and pacing accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative Approach (practical tactic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Working with an experienced screenwriter can balance strengths and produce successful adaptations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collaboration allows fidelity to source material while meeting cinematic demands. Example given: Andy Weir collaborating with 'Dew Goddard' on The Martian adaptation (article's cited example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the Choice Based on Strengths, Resources, and Time
rubrics_metrics.description: The final decision to adapt yourself or hire a professional should weigh your personal strengths, available resources, and time commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully consider your skills, ability to learn or collaborate, access to mentorship or workshops, and whether you can commit the necessary time before choosing to adapt your own novel.
